summary: Psalm 43 is a short plea from a speaker under pressure from deceitful and wicked people. The speaker asks God for vindication, admits feeling rejected and mournful, then asks God's light and truth to lead him back to worship. The psalm ends by addressing the speaker's own soul and calling it to hope in God.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows lament moving toward worship without pretending the trouble has already disappeared. It also repeats the refrain found in Psalm 42, so readers often notice Psalms 42–43 as closely linked prayers of distress and hope.

context.author: Psalms is an anthology with many writers and collections; this chapter is not assigned here to one named author.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that received the Psalms as prayer and Scripture.
context.date: Individual psalms may come from different periods from the monarchy through the postexilic era; assigning one date to the whole Psalter would be misleading.
context.setting: Book II of Psalms, where prayers of distress, sanctuary longing, and hope appear within a larger collection of worship poetry.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry and prayer, using complaint, petition, worship language, and a repeated self-addressing refrain.

outline.heading: A plea for justice
outline.note: The speaker asks God to vindicate him, plead his cause, and deliver him from deceitful and wicked people.

outline.heading: Strength felt as absence
outline.note: The speaker calls God his strength while asking why he feels rejected and must go mourning under enemy oppression.

outline.heading: Guidance back to God's dwelling
outline.note: The prayer asks for God's light and truth to lead him to the holy hill and tents.

outline.heading: Joyful worship imagined
outline.note: The speaker anticipates going to God's altar and praising God with the harp.

outline.heading: The soul addressed with hope
outline.note: The psalm ends by questioning despair and disturbance, then urging hope in God and future praise.

keyVerses.text: Vindicate me, God, and plead my cause against an ungodly nation. Oh, deliver me from deceitful and wicked men.
keyVerses.why: This opening names the chapter's immediate pressure: injustice, opposition, and a request for God to act as defender.

keyVerses.text: Oh, send out your light and your truth. Let them lead me. Let them bring me to your holy hill, to your tents.
keyVerses.why: The prayer turns from the enemies to guidance, asking God to lead the speaker back toward the place of worship.

keyVerses.text: Then I will go to the altar of God, to God, my exceeding joy. I will praise you on the harp, God, my God.
keyVerses.why: This verse shows the hoped-for result of deliverance: renewed access to worship and praise.

keyVerses.text: Why are you in despair, my soul? Why are you disturbed within me? Hope in God! For I shall still praise him: my Savior, my helper, and my God.
keyVerses.why: The final refrain holds together honest distress and deliberate hope, making it the chapter's closing emotional turn.

themes: God's light and truth as guides

questions.question: What is happening in this psalm?
questions.answer: The speaker is under pressure from deceitful and wicked people and asks God to judge in his favor. The chapter does not give a detailed story, place, or date. Its movement is from appeal, to grief, to a prayer for guidance, to anticipated worship, to renewed hope.

questions.question: What does “Vindicate me” mean here?
questions.answer: In verse 1, the speaker asks God to show him to be in the right and to take up his cause against hostile people. The legal language fits the phrases “plead my cause” and “deliver me.” The psalm does not describe the exact accusation or conflict behind the request.

questions.question: Why does the speaker say God is his strength and then ask why God has rejected him?
questions.answer: Verse 2 holds trust and distress side by side. The speaker calls God “the God of my strength,” but his experience feels like rejection because he is still mourning under enemy oppression. The psalm does not resolve that tension by explaining why the suffering continues.

questions.question: What are “your light and your truth” doing in the psalm?
questions.answer: They are pictured as guides sent by God. The speaker asks them to lead him and bring him to God's holy hill and tents. The verse does not define the terms abstractly; it shows them by their effect, guiding the speaker back toward God's presence and worship.

questions.question: What are the “holy hill” and “tents”?
questions.answer: The phrases point toward the place where the speaker expects to meet God in worship. In the Psalms, many poems are oriented toward Jerusalem and temple worship, but this verse itself uses poetic language rather than giving a map. The main point is the desired return to God's dwelling and altar.

questions.question: Why does the speaker mention the altar and harp?
questions.answer: Verse 4 imagines restored worship. The altar belongs to sacrifice and approach to God, while the harp belongs to praise. The speaker's hope is not only escape from enemies, but renewed joy before God.

questions.question: Is the psalm saying sadness is wrong?
questions.answer: No. The speaker openly says he is mourning and speaks to a soul in despair and disturbance. The final command to “Hope in God” does not erase the earlier grief; it answers it from within the prayer.

questions.question: Why does verse 5 sound familiar if someone has read Psalm 42?
questions.answer: The same refrain appears in Psalm 42, and refrains can mark emotional turns in Psalms 42–43. Readers differ on whether Psalms 42 and 43 were once one poem or are two closely connected psalms. Either way, this chapter uses the refrain to end with hope rather than silence.

questions.question: Does this chapter promise that the speaker has already been rescued?
questions.answer: Not directly. The speaker says, “I shall still praise him,” which looks forward to future praise, but the chapter ends before narrating an actual rescue. The hope is real, but the pressure named in verses 1 and 2 is not described as already gone.

glossary.def: To act in someone's favor by showing their cause to be right; in this verse, the speaker asks God to do this against hostile people.
A phrase that pictures God taking up the speaker's case, like an advocate or defender.
The place toward which the speaker wants God to lead him, associated in the verse with God's tents and worship.
The worship place the speaker hopes to reach when God leads him back.
The instrument the speaker says he will use in praise to God.
The speaker's own self addressed directly in the final verse, where despair is met with a call to hope in God.
